title: What's a "Minimum Viable Understanding" of the Five Key Beliefs?
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart lays out the theoretical groundwork a teacher or PD leader needs before doing anything practical with his five key beliefs (5KB) framework, arguing that good professional development builds shared understanding rather than shared emotion. He defines a 'minimum viable understanding' in three steps: schools exist to advance students' long-term flourishing through mastery, mastery cannot be coerced because it requires care, and the five key beliefs exist to explain and cultivate that care. He contends that teachers systematically underestimate how influenceable these beliefs are, calling this the most powerful untapped asset in classrooms worldwide. The piece functions as a conceptual on-ramp, positioning the 5KB model as a tool for doing the profession's 'one thing' rather than an additional initiative layered on top of existing work.
points: Stuart's core distinction — 'shared understandings trump shared emotions' — is a direct critique of PD that aims for a feeling in the room rather than a durable, actionable framework.

His three-step minimum viable understanding traces a causal chain: schools exist for mastery, mastery requires care, and care is what the five key beliefs are designed to cultivate — positioning 5KB as infrastructure rather than an add-on initiative.
The claim that human beings 'can't be coerced into caring' reframes classroom motivation problems as a category error when addressed with compliance-based tactics.

He asserts that teachers chronically underestimate how influenceable the five key beliefs are in the classroom, calling this blind spot 'the most powerful untapped asset in every classroom in the world.'
quotes: The goal of good PDs is the development of 1) shared understandings that 2) make a difference.
Shared understandings trump shared emotions. Sometimes you sit in a PD that seems just aimed at a feeling, but the trouble is that my thoughts last longer than my feelings.

The hardest thing about our mission — and the most beautiful thing, I think — is that mastery isn't something you can force upon somebody. You can't coerce a person into getting better at mathematics or gaining expertise at an instrument.
There are lots of ways to coerce students into doing work, but human beings just can't be coerced into caring.

Teachers tend to underestimate the degree to which these beliefs are influenceable, particularly when students are with us in the classroom. Yet, the research is clear that they are remarkably influenceable.

IMHO, this is the most powerful untapped asset in every classroom in the world — this unfortunate blindness to the degree to which these beliefs can be cultivated in a classroom and the degree to which teachers have power in doing this cultivation.
